claim: Manipulations that increase coactivation of memories sometimes lead to differentiation of these memories in hippocampal learning studies.
source: Studies of hippocampal learning have obtained seemingly contradictory results, with manipulations that increase coactivation of memories sometimes leading to differentiation of these memories, but sometimes not.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of prior research findings in the abstract.

claim: Manipulations that increase coactivation of memories sometimes do not lead to differentiation of these memories in hippocampal learning studies.
source: Studies of hippocampal learning have obtained seemingly contradictory results, with manipulations that increase coactivation of memories sometimes leading to differentiation of these memories, but sometimes not.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of prior research findings in the abstract.

claim: The nonmonotonic plasticity hypothesis posits that representational change is a U-shaped function of the coactivation of memories during learning.
source: These results could potentially be reconciled using the nonmonotonic plasticity hypothesis, which posits that representational change (memories moving apart or together) is a U-shaped function of the coactivation of these memories during learning.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the theoretical hypothesis being tested.

claim: Testing the nonmonotonic plasticity hypothesis requires manipulating coactivation over a wide enough range to reveal the full U-shape.
source: Testing this hypothesis requires manipulating coactivation over a wide enough range to reveal the full U-shape.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological requirement in the abstract.

claim: A novel neural network image synthesis procedure was used to create pairs of stimuli that varied parametrically in their similarity in high-level visual regions that provide input to the hippocampus.
source: To accomplish this, we used a novel neural network image synthesis procedure to create pairs of stimuli that varied parametrically in their similarity in high-level visual regions that provide input to the hippocampus.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach used in the study.

claim: Learning changed the representations of paired images in the dentate gyrus as a U-shaped function of image similarity.
source: As predicted, learning changed the representations of paired images in the dentate gyrus as a U-shaped function of image similarity, with neural differentiation occurring only for moderately similar images.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study as stated in the abstract.

claim: Neural differentiation occurred only for moderately similar images in the dentate gyrus.
source: As predicted, learning changed the representations of paired images in the dentate gyrus as a U-shaped function of image similarity, with neural differentiation occurring only for moderately similar images.
evidence: This is part of the main finding stated in the abstract.

claim: Experiences are encoded in distributed representations spanning populations of neurons that are partially reused across multiple memories.
source: Our experiences are encoded in distributed representations (Johnson et al., 2009; Polyn et al., 2005), spanning populations of neurons that are partially reused across multiple memories, leading to overlap.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Overlapping neural populations representing different memories in the hippocampus can shift during learning, leading to either integration or differentiation.
source: As we learn, the overlapping neural populations representing different memories in the hippocampus can shift, leading to either integration, where memories become more similar to one other, or differentiation, where memories become more distinct from one another for reviews, see Brunec et al., 2020; Duncan and Schlichting, 2018; Ritvo et al., 2019.
evidence: This is stated with citations to review articles.

claim: Integration occurs when memories become more similar to one another.
source: As we learn, the overlapping neural populations representing different memories in the hippocampus can shift, leading to either integration, where memories become more similar to one other, or differentiation, where memories become more distinct from one another for reviews, see Brunec et al., 2020; Duncan and Schlichting, 2018; Ritvo et al., 2019.
evidence: This is a definition provided in the text.

claim: Differentiation occurs when memories become more distinct from one another.
source: As we learn, the overlapping neural populations representing different memories in the hippocampus can shift, leading to either integration, where memories become more similar to one other, or differentiation, where memories become more distinct from one another for reviews, see Brunec et al., 2020; Duncan and Schlichting, 2018; Ritvo et al., 2019.
evidence: This is a definition provided in the text.

claim: Traditional Hebbian learning models hold that synaptic connections strengthen when the pre-synaptic neuron repeatedly stimulates the post-synaptic neuron.
source: Traditional Hebbian learning models hold that synaptic connections strengthen when the pre-synaptic neuron repeatedly stimulates the post-synaptic neuron, causing them to fire together (Buonomano and Merzenich, 1998; Caporale and Dan, 2008; Feldman, 2009; Hebb, 1949).
evidence: This is a statement about established theory with citations.

claim: A greater degree of coactivation among representations will strengthen shared connections and lead to integration according to Hebbian learning.
source: A greater degree of coactivation among representations will strengthen shared connections and lead to integration.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of Hebbian learning principles as described in the text.

claim: Arbitrary pairs of objects integrate in the hippocampus following repeated temporal or spatial co-occurrence.
source: Consistent with this view, arbitrary pairs of objects integrate in the hippocampus following repeated temporal or spatial co-occurrence (e.g. Deuker et al., 2016; Schapiro et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: New information that builds a link between two previously disconnected events can lead the representations of the events to integrate.
source: Moreover, new information that builds a link between two previously disconnected events can lead the representations of the events to integrate (Collin et al., 2015; Milivojevic et al., 2015; Tompary and Davachi, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Coactivation can produce differentiation in some cases.
source: In other cases, however, coactivation produces the exact opposite outcome — differentiation.
evidence: This is stated as a contrast to the Hebbian prediction.

claim: Hippocampal representations of two faces with similar associations differentiate as a result of learning.
source: For example, hippocampal representations of two faces with similar associations (Favila et al., 2016) and of two navigation events with similar routes (Chanales et al., 2017) differentiate as a result of learning.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: Hippocampal representations of two navigation events with similar routes differentiate as a result of learning.
source: For example, hippocampal representations of two faces with similar associations (Favila et al., 2016) and of two navigation events with similar routes (Chanales et al., 2017) differentiate as a result of learning.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: Some studies have found that the same experimental conditions can lead to integration in some subfields of the hippocampus and differentiation in other subfields.
source: Further complicating matters, some studies have found that the same experimental conditions can lead to integration in some subfields of the hippocampus and differentiation in other subfields (Dimsdale-Zucker et al., 2018; Molitor et al., 2021; Schlichting et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The nonmonotonic plasticity hypothesis posits low levels of coactivation between two memories will lead to no change in their overlap.
source: According to the NMPH, low levels of coactivation between two memories will lead to no change in their overlap; high levels of coactivation will strengthen mutual connections and lead to integration; and moderate levels of coactivation (where one memory is strongly active and the unique parts of the other memory are only moderately active) will weaken mutual connections and lead to differentiation, thereby reducing competition between the memories for later retrieval attempts (Hulbert and Norman, 2015; Ritvo et al., 2019; Wimber et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a description of the theoretical hypothesis with citations.

claim: The nonmonotonic plasticity hypothesis posits high levels of coactivation will strengthen mutual connections and lead to integration.
source: According to the NMPH, low levels of coactivation between two memories will lead to no change in their overlap; high levels of coactivation will strengthen mutual connections and lead to integration; and moderate levels of coactivation (where one memory is strongly active and the unique parts of the other memory are only moderately active) will weaken mutual connections and lead to differentiation, thereby reducing competition between the memories for later retrieval attempts (Hulbert and Norman, 2015; Ritvo et al., 2019; Wimber et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a description of the theoretical hypothesis with citations.

claim: The nonmonotonic plasticity hypothesis posits moderate levels of coactivation will weaken mutual connections and lead to differentiation.
source: According to the NMPH, low levels of coactivation between two memories will lead to no change in their overlap; high levels of coactivation will strengthen mutual connections and lead to integration; and moderate levels of coactivation (where one memory is strongly active and the unique parts of the other memory are only moderately active) will weaken mutual connections and lead to differentiation, thereby reducing competition between the memories for later retrieval attempts (Hulbert and Norman, 2015; Ritvo et al., 2019; Wimber et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a description of the theoretical hypothesis with citations.

claim: The NMPH has been put forward as a learning mechanism that applies broadly across tasks in which memories compete.
source: The NMPH has been put forward as a learning mechanism that applies broadly across tasks in which memories compete, whether they have been linked based on incidental co-occurrence in time or through more intentional associative learning (Ritvo et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to a prior theoretical paper.

claim: No existing study has demonstrated the full U-shaped pattern for representational change.
source: No existing study has demonstrated the full U-shaped pattern for representational change; that is what we set out to do here, using a visual statistical learning paradigm — specifically, we brought about coactivation using temporal co-occurrence between paired items, and we manipulated the degree of coactivation by varying the visual similarity of the items in a pair.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in the literature that the current study addresses.

claim: There are three factors that influence how strongly the hippocampal representation of item A coactivates with the hippocampal representation of item B during statistical learning: overlap in the high-level visual cortex representations, recurrent input from overlapping features within the hippocampus, and residual activation of item A's representation in visual cortex.
source: Crucially, the figure illustrates that there are three factors that influence how strongly the hippocampal representation of item A coactivates with the hippocampal representation of item B during statistical learning: (1) overlap in the high-level visual cortex representations of items A and B; (2) recurrent input from overlapping features within the hippocampus; and (3) residual activation of item A's representation in visual cortex (because item A was presented immediately before item B).
evidence: This is stated as a theoretical framework illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Later DNN layers correspond most closely to higher order, object-selective visual areas.
source: Most critically, later DNN layers correspond most closely to higher order, object-selective visual areas (Eickenberg et al., 2017; Güçlü and van Gerven, 2015; Jozwik et al., 2019; Khaligh-Razavi and Kriegeskorte, 2014), and when neural networks are optimized to match human performance, their higher layers predict neural responses in higher-order visual cortex (Cadieu et al., 2014; Yamins et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: When neural networks are optimized to match human performance, their higher layers predict neural responses in higher-order visual cortex.
source: Most critically, later DNN layers correspond most closely to higher order, object-selective visual areas (Eickenberg et al., 2017; Güçlü and van Gerven, 2015; Jozwik et al., 2019; Khaligh-Razavi and Kriegeskorte, 2014), and when neural networks are optimized to match human performance, their higher layers predict neural responses in higher-order visual cortex (Cadieu et al., 2014; Yamins et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The intended and actual similarity levels of the images in terms of model features showed a close correspondence.
source: We found that the intended and actual similarity levels of the images (in terms of model features) showed a close correspondence (Figure 2—figure supplement 2): In the highest four layers (4D-5B), the intended and actual feature correlations were strongly associated (r(62) = .970, .983, .977, .985, respectively).
evidence: This is a validation result with specific correlation values reported.

claim: In the highest four layers of the Inception model, the intended and actual feature correlations were strongly associated (r(62) = .970, .983, .977, .985, respectively).
source: We found that the intended and actual similarity levels of the images (in terms of model features) showed a close correspondence (Figure 2—figure supplement 2): In the highest four layers (4D-5B), the intended and actual feature correlations were strongly associated (r(62) = .970, .983, .977, .985, respectively).
evidence: This is a specific quantitative result from the model validation.

claim: In the lower and middle layers of the Inception model, feature correlations did not vary across pairs, as intended.
source: In the lower and middle layers, feature correlations did not vary across pairs, as intended.
evidence: This is a validation result confirming the intended design.

claim: Perceptual distance was strongly negatively associated with the intended model similarity (r(62) = −0.813, p < 0.0001).
source: When further averaged across participants, perceptual distance was strongly negatively associated with the intended model similarity (r(62) = −0.813, p < 0.0001; Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the behavioral validation study.

claim: Every individual participant's correlation between perceptual distance and model similarity was negative (mean r = −0.552, 95% CI = [−0.593–0.512]).
source: In fact, every individual participant's correlation was negative (mean r = −0.552, 95% CI = [−0.593–0.512]).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the behavioral validation study.

claim: Model similarity level was positively associated with neural similarity in LO (mean r = 0.182, 95% CI = [0.083 0.279], randomization p = 0.007).
source: Model similarity level was positively associated with neural similarity in LO (mean r = 0.182, 95% CI = [0.083 0.279], randomization p = 0.007) and PHC (mean r = 0.125, 95% CI = [0.022 0.228], p = 0.029).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the neural validation analysis.

claim: Model similarity level was positively associated with neural similarity in PHC (mean r = 0.125, 95% CI = [0.022 0.228], p = 0.029).
source: Model similarity level was positively associated with neural similarity in LO (mean r = 0.182, 95% CI = [0.083 0.279], randomization p = 0.007) and PHC (mean r = 0.125, 95% CI = [0.022 0.228], p = 0.029).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the neural validation analysis.

claim: V1 showed a negative relationship between model similarity and neural similarity (mean r = −0.112, 95% CI = [−0.224–0.003], p = .038).
source: V1 showed a negative relationship (mean r = −0.112, 95% CI = [−0.224–0.003], p = .038).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the neural validation analysis.

claim: The searchlight analysis revealed two large clusters of voxels where neural similarity was positively associated with model similarity: left ventral and dorsal LO extending into posterior FG and right ventral and dorsal LO extending into occipital pole.
source: This revealed two large clusters of voxels (p < 0.05 corrected): left ventral and dorsal LO extending into posterior FG (3722 voxels; peak t-value = 5.60; MNI coordinates of peak = −37.5,–72.0, −10.5; coordinates of center = −26.7,–71.7, 17.4) and right ventral and dorsal LO extending into occipital pole (3107 voxels; peak t-value = 4.82; coordinates of peak = 33.0, –88.5, 10.5; coordinates of center = 30.9, –86.5, 10.6).
evidence: This is a result from the whole-brain searchlight analysis with specific anatomical locations and statistics.

claim: The predictions of the theory-constrained cubic model were reliably associated with representational change in DG (r = 0.134, 95% CI = [0.007 0.267], randomization p = 0.022).
source: The predictions of this theory-constrained cubic model were reliably associated with representational change in DG (r = 0.134, 95% CI = [0.007 0.267], randomization p = 0.022).
evidence: This is the main finding of the representational change analysis.

claim: The cubic model fit was not reliable in CA2/3 (r = 0.082, 95% CI = [−0.027 0.191], p = 0.13).
evidence: This is a negative result from the representational change analysis.

claim: The cubic model fit was not reliable in CA1 (r = 0.116, 95% CI = [−0.001 0.231], p = 0.10).
evidence: This is a negative result from the representational change analysis.

claim: The cubic model fit was not reliable in the hippocampus as a whole (r = 0.084, 95% CI = [−0.018 0.186], p = 0.15).
evidence: This is a negative result from the representational change analysis.

claim: The whole-brain searchlight analysis revealed two reliable clusters: right hippocampus extending into PHC and FG, and anterior cingulate extending into medial prefrontal cortex.
source: This analysis revealed two reliable clusters (p < 0.05 corrected): right hippocampus extending into PHC and FG (832 voxels; peak t-value = 4.97; MNI coordinates of peak = 37.5,–7.5, −15.0; coordinates of center = 32.8,–18.7, −17.1) and anterior cingulate, extending into medial prefrontal cortex (1604 voxels; peak t-value = 5.43; coordinates of peak = −7.5, 28.5, 21.0; coordinates of center = −5.0, 28.5, 10.2).
evidence: This is a result from the whole-brain searchlight analysis with specific anatomical locations and statistics.

claim: The degree of overlap in visual features determined the nature of representational change in DG.
source: We set out to determine how learning shapes representations in the hippocampus and found that the degree of overlap in visual features determined the nature of representational change in DG.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main finding in the Discussion.

claim: With low or high overlap, object representations did not reliably change with respect to one another in DG.
source: The pattern of results was U-shaped: with low or high overlap, object representations did not reliably change with respect to one another, whereas with moderate overlap, they pushed apart from one another following learning.
evidence: This is a summary of the U-shaped pattern observed in the data.

claim: With moderate overlap, object representations pushed apart from one another following learning in DG.
source: The pattern of results was U-shaped: with low or high overlap, object representations did not reliably change with respect to one another, whereas with moderate overlap, they pushed apart from one another following learning.
evidence: This is a summary of the U-shaped pattern observed in the data.

claim: The present study is the first to span coactivation continuously in order to reveal the full U-shape predicted by the NMPH.
source: Crucially, the present study is the first to span coactivation continuously in order to reveal the full U-shape predicted by the NMPH, whereby differentiation emerges as coactivation grows from low to moderate and dissipates as coactivation continues from moderate to high.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the current study.

claim: This is the first demonstration of the efficacy of stimulus synthesis in manipulating high-level representational similarity in targeted brain regions in humans.
source: This is the first demonstration of the efficacy of stimulus synthesis in manipulating high-level representational similarity in targeted brain regions in humans.
evidence: This is a claim about the methodological novelty of the study.

claim: Hippocampal neurons encode complex information from multiple sensory modalities.
source: Numerous studies have shown that, while hippocampal neurons are indeed 'downstream' from visual cortex, they additionally encode complex information from multiple sensory modalities (Lavenex and Amaral, 2000), as well as information about reward (Wimmer and Shohamy, 2012), social relevance (Olson et al., 2007), context (Turk-Browne et al., 2012), and time (Hsieh et al., 2014; Schapiro et al., 2012), to name a few.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Hippocampal neurons encode information about reward.
source: Numerous studies have shown that, while hippocampal neurons are indeed 'downstream' from visual cortex, they additionally encode complex information from multiple sensory modalities (Lavenex and Amaral, 2000), as well as information about reward (Wimmer and Shohamy, 2012), social relevance (Olson et al., 2007), context (Turk-Browne et al., 2012), and time (Hsieh et al., 2014; Schapiro et al., 2012), to name a few.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study.

source: Numerous studies have shown that, while hippocampal neurons are indeed 'downstream' from visual cortex, they additionally encode complex information from multiple sensory modalities (Lavenex and Amaral, 2000), as well as information about reward (Wimmer and Shohamy, 2012), social relevance (Olson et al., 2007), context (Turk-Browne et al., 2012), and time (Hsieh et al., 2014; Schapiro et al., 2012), to name a few.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study.

source: Numerous studies have shown that, while hippocampal neurons are indeed 'downstream' from visual cortex, they additionally encode complex information from multiple sensory modalities (Lavenex and Amaral, 2000), as well as information about reward (Wimmer and Shohamy, 2012), social relevance (Olson et al., 2007), context (Turk-Browne et al., 2012), and time (Hsieh et al., 2014; Schapiro et al., 2012), to name a few.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study.

source: Numerous studies have shown that, while hippocampal neurons are indeed 'downstream' from visual cortex, they additionally encode complex information from multiple sensory modalities (Lavenex and Amaral, 2000), as well as information about reward (Wimmer and Shohamy, 2012), social relevance (Olson et al., 2007), context (Turk-Browne et al., 2012), and time (Hsieh et al., 2014; Schapiro et al., 2012), to name a few.

claim: Prior work has shown hippocampal differentiation in experimental conditions involving faces and scenes.
source: Prior work has shown hippocampal differentiation in experimental conditions involving faces and scenes (Favila et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2014; Kim et al., 2017) as well as complex navigation events (Chanales et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Prior work has shown hippocampal differentiation in experimental conditions involving complex navigation events.
source: Prior work has shown hippocampal differentiation in experimental conditions involving faces and scenes (Favila et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2014; Kim et al., 2017) as well as complex navigation events (Chanales et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: The differentiation 'dip' creating the U shape was reliable in DG.
source: We found that the differentiation 'dip' (creating the U shape) was reliable in DG.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main finding.

claim: Prior studies found differentiation in a combined CA2/3/DG ROI.
source: This fits with prior studies that found differentiation in a combined CA2/3/DG ROI (Dimsdale-Zucker et al., 2018; Kim et al., 2017; Molitor et al., 2021), and greater sparsity and pattern separation in DG in particular (Berron et al., 2016; GoodSmith et al., 2017; Leutgeb et al., 2007), although note that the U-shaped pattern was trending but not significant in CA2/3 in our study.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Prior studies found greater sparsity and pattern separation in DG in particular.
source: This fits with prior studies that found differentiation in a combined CA2/3/DG ROI (Dimsdale-Zucker et al., 2018; Kim et al., 2017; Molitor et al., 2021), and greater sparsity and pattern separation in DG in particular (Berron et al., 2016; GoodSmith et al., 2017; Leutgeb et al., 2007), although note that the U-shaped pattern was trending but not significant in CA2/3 in our study.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The U-shaped pattern was trending but not significant in CA2/3 in the current study.
source: This fits with prior studies that found differentiation in a combined CA2/3/DG ROI (Dimsdale-Zucker et al., 2018; Kim et al., 2017; Molitor et al., 2021), and greater sparsity and pattern separation in DG in particular (Berron et al., 2016; GoodSmith et al., 2017; Leutgeb et al., 2007), although note that the U-shaped pattern was trending but not significant in CA2/3 in our study.
evidence: This is a statement about the results in CA2/3.

claim: CA2/3 and DG show much sparser codes than CA1.
source: Prior work has shown that there is extensive variation in overall activity (sparsity) levels across hippocampal subfields, with CA2/3 and DG showing much sparser codes than CA1 (Barnes et al., 1990; Duncan and Schlichting, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Human fMRI studies have found that CA1 is relatively biased toward integration and CA2/3/DG are relatively biased toward differentiation.
source: Consistent with this idea, human fMRI studies have found that CA1 is relatively biased toward integration and CA2/3/DG are relatively biased toward differentiation (Dimsdale-Zucker et al., 2018; Kim et al., 2017; Molitor et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: DG shows sparser activity than CA3.
source: First, DG shows sparser activity than CA3 (Barnes et al., 1990; GoodSmith et al., 2017; West et al., 1991) and thus will do a better job of sampling the left side of the coactivation curve.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: CA3 is known to show strong attractor dynamics ('pattern completion').
source: Second, CA3 is known to show strong attractor dynamics ('pattern completion'; Guzowski et al., 2004; McNaughton and Morris, 1987; Rolls and Treves, 1998) that might make it difficult to observe moderate levels of coactivation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Rodent studies have demonstrated that CA3 patterns tend to sharply flip between one pattern and the other rather than coactivating representations of different locations.
source: For example, rodent studies have demonstrated that, rather than coactivating representations of different locations, CA3 patterns tend to sharply flip between one pattern and the other (e.g. Leutgeb et al., 2007; Vazdarjanova and Guzowski, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior rodent studies.

claim: The results are broadly consistent with prior findings that increasing the coactivation of memories can lead to differentiation.
source: Although our results are broadly consistent with prior findings that increasing the coactivation of memories can lead to differentiation (Chanales et al., 2017; Favila et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2017; Schlichting et al., 2015), they are notably inconsistent with results from Schapiro et al., 2012, who reported memory integration for arbitrarily paired images as a result of temporal co-occurrence; pairs in our study with comparable levels of visual similarity (roughly model similarity level 3) showed no evidence of integration.
evidence: This is a comparison to prior literature with citations.

claim: The results are notably inconsistent with results from Schapiro et al., 2012, who reported memory integration for arbitrarily paired images as a result of temporal co-occurrence.
source: Although our results are broadly consistent with prior findings that increasing the coactivation of memories can lead to differentiation (Chanales et al., 2017; Favila et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2017; Schlichting et al., 2015), they are notably inconsistent with results from Schapiro et al., 2012, who reported memory integration for arbitrarily paired images as a result of temporal co-occurrence; pairs in our study with comparable levels of visual similarity (roughly model similarity level 3) showed no evidence of integration.
evidence: This is a comparison to prior literature with a citation.

claim: Pairs in the current study with comparable levels of visual similarity to Schapiro et al., 2012 (roughly model similarity level 3) showed no evidence of integration.
source: Although our results are broadly consistent with prior findings that increasing the coactivation of memories can lead to differentiation (Chanales et al., 2017; Favila et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2017; Schlichting et al., 2015), they are notably inconsistent with results from Schapiro et al., 2012, who reported memory integration for arbitrarily paired images as a result of temporal co-occurrence; pairs in our study with comparable levels of visual similarity (roughly model similarity level 3) showed no evidence of integration.
evidence: This is a comparison of the current results to prior work.

claim: Each functional run contained 203 volumes.
source: Each run contained 203 volumes.
evidence: This describes the fMRI acquisition parameters.

claim: The automatic segmentation of hippocampal subfields (ASHS) software package was used to derive participant-specific medial temporal lobe regions of interest.
source: For each participant, their T1- and T2-weighted anatomical images were submitted to the automatic segmentation of hippocampal subfields (ASHS) software package (Yushkevich et al., 2015), to derive participant-specific medial temporal lobe regions of interest.
evidence: This describes the ROI definition method with a citation.

claim: An atlas containing 51 manual segmentations of hippocampal subfields was used for ASHS segmentation.
source: We used an atlas containing 51 manual segmentations of hippocampal subfields (Aly and Turk-Browne, 2016a; Aly and Turk-Browne, 2016b).
evidence: This describes the atlas used with citations.

claim: Freesurfer was used to create masks for V1, V2, lateral occipital (LO) cortex, fusiform gyrus (FG), parahippocampal cortex (PHC), and inferior temporal (IT) cortex.
source: For visual ROIs, freesurfer (http://surfer.nmr.mgh.harvard.edu/) was used to create masks for V1, V2, lateral occipital (LO) cortex, fusiform gyrus (FG), parahippocampal cortex (PHC), and inferior temporal (IT) cortex, for each participant.
evidence: This describes the ROI definition method for visual regions.
